HomeEssentials Inc. - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the HomeEssentials Inc. Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, instructions for queuing up will be given at that time. Please also note, today's event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss HomeEssentials Inc.'s results for the Q3 2024. Joining me on today’s call are Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; David Thompson, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Merchandising Officer; Robert Hayes, Chief Stores Officer; and Emily Vargas, Chief Marketing Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

With that, I’ll turn the call over to Michael Reynolds.

Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you, Sarah. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I’m pleased to report HomeEssentials Inc.'s performance for the Q3 2024. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities and delivered solid results despite the challenging macroeconomic environment.

Today I will cover seven key aspects of our performance. First, our marketing and advertising expense trends reflect smart investments yielding strong returns. Second, we've advanced strategies for inventory optimization that are protecting margins and boosting efficiency. Third, inventory levels showed meaningful improvement year-over-year. Fourth, key strategic initiatives are progressing well across omnichannel and store optimization. Fifth, our store footprint saw disciplined openings and closings. Sixth, labor costs and store payroll delivered impressive leverage. And seventh, we've made progress mitigating the impact of shrink and theft on gross margins.

We are confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value for our shareholders.

Now, I'll turn the call over to David Thompson to provide more details on our financial results.

David Thompson, Chief Financial Officer:
Thank you, Michael. Good morning. I'll provide a more detailed review of our financial performance for the Q3 2024.

Our total revenue for the quarter was $3.52 billion, a 5.2% increase compared to the same period last year, driven by 4.1% comparable store sales growth and digital channel expansion.

Gross margin was 38.5%, expanding 220 basis points year-over-year, primarily driven by lower shrink rates, optimized markdowns, and favorable product mix shifts.

Operating expenses were $1.2 billion, representing 34.1% of revenue, with leverage from higher sales volume and productivity gains.

Net income was $165 million, or $0.92 per share.

We generated $420 million in cash flow from operations.

Inventory levels are currently $1.18 billion, down 12% year-over-year, reflecting disciplined management.

We are maintaining a strong balance sheet and are well positioned to invest in our growth initiatives.

Let me expand on several critical areas starting with marketing and advertising expense trends. Marketing and advertising expenses came in at $148 million for the quarter, up 8% year-over-year from $137 million in Q3 2023. As a percentage of net sales, this represented 4.2%, a slight expansion from 4.0% last year but flat sequentially from Q2 2024's 4.2%. This modest increase reflects our deliberate investments in high-ROI omnichannel strategies to drive foot traffic to our 1,200-plus brick-and-mortar locations while accelerating digital commerce growth, which now accounts for 28% of total sales—up from 22% a year ago.

Breaking it down by channel, total digital advertising spend surged 22% year-over-year to $92 million, comprising 62% of our marketing budget, compared to just 48% in Q3 2023. This shift highlights the retail industry's move away from linear TV and print, which we've deprioritized—those legacy channels now make up only 12% of spend, down from 22%. Our programmatic video and display investments via platforms like Google DV360 and The Trade Desk delivered a blended ROAS of 4.8x, a 25% improvement year-over-year, thanks to enhanced first-party data from our HomeEssentials Rewards loyalty program, which boasts 45 million active members. We're leveraging clean rooms with partners like LiveRamp to activate this data compliantly under CCPA and GDPR, focusing on lookalike modeling to lower customer acquisition costs by 15% to $28 per new customer.

Social media and retail media networks were standout performers. Meta platforms like Facebook and Instagram, along with TikTok, drove 35% of our digital impressions, with shoppable posts tied to in-store pickup boosting conversion rates by 18% for high-margin categories like kitchen appliances and outdoor living products. Our partnership with the HomeEssentials Retail Media Network—launched last year with Criteo—generated $42 million in ad revenue from CPG brands like Procter & Gamble and Unilever, effectively subsidizing 28% of our total marketing spend. This aligns with industry trends seen at peers like Target with Roundel and Walmart Connect, where retail media is projected to reach $100 billion by 2026 according to eMarketer.

On the brick-and-mortar side, we're blending digital with physical through geofencing and hyperlocal activations. Spend here grew 12% to $32 million, emphasizing digital out-of-home screens in high-traffic malls and our store-front experiential hubs. For example, our 'Build Your Backyard' AR-enabled campaign, promoted via Snapchat lenses and in-store QR codes, lifted same-store sales in outdoor categories by 14% in Q3. Attribution modeling via our proprietary multi-touch platform shows these efforts yielding a 3.5x ROAS, with a clear halo effect on average order value, which rose to $145 from $138 year-over-year.

Regionally, in the U.S., which represents 72% of our sales, marketing efficiency was strongest—expenses as a percentage of sales dipped to 3.9% amid robust suburban demand for home improvement, fueled by housing starts up 7% per Census Bureau data. We ramped connected TV spend on platforms like Roku and Hulu by 30%, targeting cord-cutters with dynamic creative optimization for regional inventory like Weber grills. Europe, at 18% of sales, saw a 5% year-over-year expense increase to €28 million equivalent, pressured by iOS privacy changes and the DMA's cookie deprecation, but offset by strong performance in the UK via ASOS Marketplace cross-promotions. Asia-Pacific, our 10% growth engine, held expenses flat at $12 million AUD equivalent, with WeChat mini-programs and KOL influencer campaigns in China driving 25% traffic uplift to stores in Shanghai and Guangzhou amid post-COVID revenge spending.

These trends underscore our 'Store-to-Web' thesis: every dollar in marketing is optimized for lifetime value expansion, with LTV:CAC now at 4.2x versus 3.6x last year. We've piloted AI-driven personalization with Salesforce Einstein, predicting cart abandonment with 87% accuracy and retargeting via SMS for in-store fulfillment, which reduced churn by 11%. Looking forward, we expect Q4 marketing spend to rise 10-12% year-over-year to support our holiday 'Essentials Everywhere' campaign, including experiential pop-ups in 50 key markets and a $20 million CTV push ahead of Prime Day rivals. Marketing expense per store visit is down 9% to $4.20—and it directly fueled our 6% comp sales growth.

Next, on strategies for inventory optimization, we've delivered a 28% reduction in excess inventory quarter-over-quarter, which directly contributed to our gross margin expansion. Coming out of prior supply chain bottlenecks like port delays in Asia and Red Sea disruptions, our inventory turnover was 4.2x for FY 2023, with days of inventory on hand averaging 82 days across our 1,200-plus stores. Shrinkage hovered at 1.8% of sales from theft in urban spots and markdowns on seasonal overstocks. Today, we've boosted turnover to 6.1x, cut DOH to 54 days, and reduced shrinkage to 1.4%, freeing up $450 million in working capital year-to-date for store remodels and digital initiatives.

Our approach blends advanced tech with retail tactics at the SKU level for our 150,000-plus stock-keeping units in apparel, home goods, and consumer electronics. First, AI-powered demand sensing and forecasting via Blue Yonder's platform integrates POS data, weather APIs, and macro signals like CPI, improving accuracy from 72% to 91% at the store-SKU-week level. In apparel, we cut stockouts on women's activewear by 35% and safety stock by 22%.

Second, omnichannel fulfillment: BOPIS hit 18% of digital sales, up from 12%, supported by Manhattan Associates' WMS with RFID in 70% of DCs and top stores, cutting cycle times by 40% and lifting fill rates to 97% in regions like the Southeast U.S.

Third, supplier collaboration with VMI and JIT for top vendors like P&G and Nike reduced lead times to 21 days amid tariff volatility. In Europe, JIT with Unilever cut excess in perishables by 32%, aiding sustainability.

Regionally, U.S. Northeast and California use ABC analysis for daily replen on A-items, dropping fashion overstock 25%. Midwest factors NOAA data for 19% DOH reduction. Internationally, UK/Germany nearshoring boosted GMROI to 178%; Asia micro-fulfillment centers target 1.5 more turns by FY 2025.

With $120 million in IoT and automation, 85% of stores have EAS with computer vision; PROS dynamic pricing reduced markdowns to 18% off, preserving $180 million in margins. GMROI is now 4.8x, ahead of Target's benchmark. Q4 pilots for AMRs and blockchain will push to 7x turnover by end-2025.

Tying into that, our inventory levels ended the quarter at $1.18 billion, a disciplined 12% year-over-year decline from $1.34 billion in Q3 last year—our sixth straight quarter of reduction, supporting 220 bps gross margin expansion and turns up 18% to 5.2x annualized.

By category, hardlines like appliances and outdoor goods dropped 18% to $620 million after clearing overstocks; softlines like bedding fell 9% to $380 million; consumables held a 3% reduction to $180 million for 96% in-stock rates.

Regionally, Sunbelt markets (55% of 1,200 stores) saw 15% drawdown with 7.2% comps; Northeast/Midwest 8% decline from weather; Canada flat as we tune assortments.

Underpinned by Blue Yonder AI (forecast accuracy +28%), RFID at 85% of SKUs (shrink -15%), VMI/JIT compressing leads to 28 days. We've rationalized SKUs 12% to 45,000 high-GMROI items, using stores for 22% of digital BOPIS. Q4 plans controlled 5-7% build for holidays at 52 DOH, ahead of sector average.

Now, an update on key strategic initiatives under our "StoreForward 2025" strategy: omnichannel acceleration, asset-light optimization, and tech-enabled operations across 1,200 stores.

Omnichannel: BOPIS/Ship-from-Store at 28% of digital sales (vs. NRF 22%), driving 15% digital fulfillment growth and 2.2 points to 4.1% comps. Targeting 35% BOPIS by 2025 with curbside to 85% of fleet; pilots lift conversions 18%.

Asset-light: Remodeled 45 stores with experiential zones, delivering 12% comp lift, 8% ticket via 42% private-label sales (target 50%). Shuttered 18 underperformers for $45M lease savings; opening 22 in Sunbelt with 15% IRR.

Tech: $250M in RetailMax Edge—RFID at 95% cuts shrink to 1.1%; AI pricing on 1.2M SKUs adds 3% margin; labor productivity +14%; LED/HVAC saves $22M, GreenRewards at 14M members.

Sunbelt comps +6.8% on housing; Midwest headwinds; Canada +3.2%. Positions for mid-single EPS growth, 55/45 physical-digital mix by 2027, $650-700M capex.

On store footprint, we opened 12 new stores and closed 9 in Q3, net +3 to 1,268 locations. YTD: 28 opens (+15% YoY), 22 closes (flat), net +6—better than peers' closures.

Southeast (35%, 442 stores): 5 opens in Charlotte etc. with BOPIS zones; 1 close. Southwest (28%, 355): 4 opens in Phoenix/DFW micro-formats; 3 closes. Midwest (20%, 254): 2 opens, 4 closes. Northeast/West (17%, 217): 1 open, 1 close.

Openings target $15M NPV; closures recapture 85% sales. Pipeline: 45 FY2025 opens (smaller formats), 25-30 closes for net +15-20, 3-5% growth. $250-300M capex.

Labor costs and store payroll showed leverage, with store labor at 11.4% of sales, down 70 bps from 12.1% YoY—adding 25 bps to SG&A deleverage, EBITDA to 8.2% (+90 bps). Absolute payroll up 1.2% to $285M on 4.8% comps; sales per labor hour $185 (+3.5%), ahead of peers.

Wages steady at $18.75 (+2.1%); 35% variable pay; FTE flat at 42,000. UKG AI scheduling cuts overstaffing 12%; self-checkout 85%, mobile POS 28%. Sunbelt deleveraged 110 bps; CA/Northeast 40 bps with flex pools.

BOPIS 18% reallocates payroll; targeting 50-75 bps more deleverage FY2025.

Finally, on shrink/theft impact, gross margin hit 38.2% (+10 bps YoY) despite 45 bps compression from shrink at 1.65% of sales ($185M loss) vs. 1.42% last year—above 1.4% target. External theft (ORC) 52%, internal 28%, admin 20%; apparel/health >2.5%.

Urban rates 2.3% (policy headwinds); Sunbelt <1.2%; Canada 1.3%. $120M in LP tech: AI vision (theft -18%), RFID 80%, EAS upgrades, basket analysis in self-checkout for 25 bps tailwind. BOPIS cuts exposure 30%. Targeting 1.35% shrink, 20 bps accretion.

We're maintaining a strong balance sheet...

Now, I'd like to hand it over to Lisa Chen, our Chief Merchandising Officer, to discuss our new product lines, followed by Robert Hayes to discuss store operations, and then Emily Vargas to discuss marketing initiatives.

Lisa Chen, Chief Merchandising Officer:
Thank you, David. This quarter, we launched our EcoHome sustainable product line, which has seen strong uptake with 20% sell-through in the first month and positive feedback on margins. We're excited about the potential of this new line and other upcoming launches in private-label essentials.

Robert Hayes, Chief Stores Officer:
Thank you, Lisa. We continue to focus on improving the customer experience in our stores. We have implemented self-checkout expansion and AI planogram optimization, and we're seeing positive results with conversion rates up 5% and labor efficiency gains.

Emily Vargas, Chief Marketing Officer:
Thank you, Robert. Our new marketing campaign, Home Refresh, has increased brand awareness by 15%, particularly through CTV and social integrations that drive omnichannel traffic.

Now, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. Instructions for questions will now be repeated. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of inflation on your sales?

Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer:
Thanks, John. Inflation has pressured discretionary spending, but our value-focused assortments and loyalty program have helped us gain share, with comps holding at 4.1% despite broader softness. Our pricing discipline and private-label growth mitigated much of the pass-through.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Maria Lopez with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Maria Lopez (JPMorgan):
What are your expectations for same-store sales growth in the next quarter?

David Thompson, Chief Financial Officer:
Good question, Maria. We're guiding to 3-5% comp growth in Q4, supported by holiday builds, marketing ramps, and inventory agility. Traffic stabilization and BOPIS strength should offset any macro softening.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Alex Patel with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Alex Patel (Morgan Stanley):
Can you elaborate on the supply chain improvements?

Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer:
Absolutely, Alex. Our JIT and VMI with key vendors, plus AI forecasting, have cut lead times significantly and reduced excess stock. Regional localization and micro-fulfillment are key, positioning us well for holiday demand without the bloat we saw previously.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Karen Wu with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Karen Wu (Barclays):
What is the impact from the loyalty program?

Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer:
Karen, the HomeEssentials Rewards program with 45 million members is a powerhouse, driving higher retention, better data for personalization, and 18% uplift in conversions via targeted offers. It's subsidizing marketing and boosting AOV meaningfully.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Tom Rivera with Citi. Please go ahead.

Tom Rivera (Citi):
Thanks. On shrink, what incremental steps are you taking beyond what's been mentioned?

David Thompson, Chief Financial Officer:
Tom, we're accelerating AI computer vision rollout to 80% of stores by year-end and enhancing self-checkout with basket analysis. Early results show 18% theft reduction, and we expect this to deliver the 20 bps margin tailwind we guided.

Operator:
Thank you. That concludes the question-and-answer session. I'll now turn the call back over to Michael Reynolds for closing remarks.

Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, we are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our long-term strategy. Thank you for your continued support.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
This concludes today's call. Thank you for joining us.
